title: Data presentation
summary: Raw data is just a list until you organise it. This lesson turns lists into [[frequency-table|frequency tables]] and [[histogram|histograms]], reads medians, quartiles and [[percentile|percentiles]] off a [[cumulative-frequency|cumulative frequency]] graph, and uses [[box-and-whisker-diagram|box and whisker diagrams]] to compare data sets.

goals.text: Put discrete and continuous data into a frequency table, with [[class-interval|class intervals]] written as inequalities with no gaps.
Draw and read a frequency histogram with equal class widths, and describe its shape.
Use a cumulative frequency graph to estimate the median, quartiles, percentiles, range and IQR.
Draw and read a box and whisker diagram, with outliers as crosses.
Compare two distributions from their box plots, and judge from symmetry whether data may be normal.

before.prompt: Which of these is discrete data?
before.hint: Is each one counted or measured?

options.text: The time taken to run $100$ m
The number of goals in a match

before.explain: Goals are counted, so they are discrete. Time and mass are measured, so they are continuous. Revise it in {{lesson:4.1}}.

before.prompt: A data set has $Q_{1} = 12$ and $Q_{3} = 20$. Find the upper fence, $Q_{3} + 1.5 \times \mathrm{IQR}$.
before.explain: $\mathrm{IQR} = 20 - 12 = 8$, so the upper fence is $20 + 1.5 \times 8 = 32$. Revise it in {{lesson:4.1}}.

before.prompt: The lower fence of a data set is $18$. Is a value of exactly $18$ an outlier?

options.text: Yes, because it lies on the fence
No, because an outlier must be less than $18$

before.explain: An outlier lies strictly beyond a fence, and $18 < 18$ is false. So $18$ is not an outlier. Revise it in {{lesson:4.1}}.

blocks.text: A list of $25$ numbers is hard to take in. Count how often each value appears, and the pattern shows at once.

blocks.statement: The [[frequency|frequency]] of a value is the number of times it occurs in the data. A [[frequency-table|frequency table]] lists each value, or each group of values, beside its frequency.

blocks.text: For [[discrete-data|discrete data]] with only a few different values, give each value its own column. Tally the list once, then count the marks.

blocks.question: A café records how many cakes are left unsold at closing time on $25$ days: $2, 1, 0, 3, 1, 2, 4, 1, 0, 2, 3, 1, 5, 2, 0, 1, 3, 2, 1, 4, 3, 0, 2, 1, 3$. Present the data in a frequency table.
steps: The values run from $0$ to $5$, so the table needs a column for each of $0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$.
Go through the list once, making a tally mark under each value. Cross off each number as you go, so none is counted twice.
$\begin{array}{c|cccccc} \text{cakes left} & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\ \hline \text{frequency} & 4 & 7 & 6 & 5 & 2 & 1 \end{array}$
Check the total: $4 + 7 + 6 + 5 + 2 + 1 = 25$, one for each day.

blocks.text: [[continuous-data|Continuous data]] is different. Measured values are rarely equal, so you group them into classes instead.

blocks.statement: A [[class-interval|class interval]] is a group of values written as an inequality, such as $20 \le t < 25$. Its ends are the lower and upper boundaries. The class width is upper boundary minus lower boundary.
blocks.plain: A class is a bucket. The inequality says exactly which values fall in it.

blocks.text: Classes must leave no gaps. With classes $20$–$24$ and $25$–$29$, a time of $24.6$ has nowhere to go. With $20 \le t < 25$ and $25 \le t < 30$, every time lands in exactly one class.
A value on a boundary goes in the class whose inequality it satisfies. Here $25$ goes in $25 \le t < 30$. Some tables use the form $10 < t \le 15$ instead, so read the signs each time.

steps: Sort out the boundary values first. $25.0$ goes in $25 \le t < 30$, $30.0$ in $30 \le t < 35$ and $35.0$ in $35 \le t < 40$.
$24.9$ is less than $25$, so it goes in $20 \le t < 25$.
Tally the rest, then count.
$\begin{array}{c|c} \text{time, } t \text{ minutes} & \text{frequency} \\ \hline 20 \le t < 25 & 5 \\ 25 \le t < 30 & 9 \\ 30 \le t < 35 & 7 \\ 35 \le t < 40 & 3 \end{array}$
Check: $5 + 9 + 7 + 3 = 24$ runners.

blocks.prompt: A runner finishes in exactly $35.0$ minutes. Using the classes in the fun run table, which class does the time belong to?
blocks.explain: $35 < 35$ is false, so $35$ is not in $30 \le t < 35$. It satisfies $35 \le t < 40$, and it belongs to that class only.

blocks.prompt: The masses of $32$ parcels are grouped into the classes $0 < m \le 2$, $2 < m \le 4$, $4 < m \le 6$ and $6 < m \le 8$ kg. The frequencies are $9$, $p$, $7$ and $4$. Find $p$.
blocks.hint: The frequencies add up to the number of parcels.

blocks.text: A table gives you numbers. A picture shows where the data bunches up, and whether it trails off to one side.

blocks.statement: A [[histogram|histogram]] draws each class as a bar on a continuous scale. The bar runs from the lower to the upper boundary, and its height is the frequency. Neighbouring bars touch.
blocks.plain: A bar chart for grouped data, with no gaps, because the scale has no gaps.

blocks.text: In this course every class in a histogram has the same width. So a taller bar always means more values.

blocks.question: Draw a frequency histogram for the fun run times. $\begin{array}{c|c} \text{time, } t \text{ minutes} & \text{frequency} \\ \hline 20 \le t < 25 & 5 \\ 25 \le t < 30 & 9 \\ 30 \le t < 35 & 7 \\ 35 \le t < 40 & 3 \end{array}$
steps: Horizontal axis: time, $t$ minutes, from $20$ to $40$, with a mark at each class boundary.
Vertical axis: frequency, from $0$ to $10$, with an even scale. The largest frequency, $9$, fits.
Draw each bar from its lower to its upper boundary, as tall as its frequency: $5$, $9$, $7$ and $3$. The bars touch.

blocks.alt: Frequency histogram of the 24 fun run times. The horizontal axis shows time from 20 to 40 minutes and the vertical axis shows frequency from 0 to 10. Four touching bars have heights 5, 9, 7 and 3.
blocks.caption: The bars touch: $25 \le t < 30$ starts exactly where $20 \le t < 25$ ends.

blocks.text: Now look at the shape. If the two sides roughly mirror each other, the data is symmetric. If one side trails off in a long tail, the data is [[skewed-distribution|skewed]].
A long tail to the right is positive skew, and a long tail to the left is negative skew. Symmetric, bell-shaped data may follow the normal distribution of {{lesson:4.9}}.

blocks.alt: Frequency histogram of the waiting times of 50 patients. The horizontal axis shows waiting time from 0 to 60 minutes in classes of 10 minutes, each including its lower end and excluding its upper end. The bar heights are 5, 12, 15, 9, 6 and 3.
blocks.caption: Waiting times at a clinic. The tail on the right is longer.

blocks.question: The histogram shows the waiting times, $w$ minutes, of $50$ patients at a clinic. The classes are $0 \le w < 10$, $10 \le w < 20$, $\ldots$, $50 \le w < 60$. (a) Find the number of patients who waited at least $30$ minutes. (b) Describe the shape of the distribution.
steps: (a) “At least $30$” means the three bars from $30$ to $60$. Read their heights: $9$, $6$ and $3$.
Add them: $9 + 6 + 3 = 18$ patients.
(b) The bars rise to a peak at $20$–$30$, then fall away slowly to $60$. The long tail is on the right, so the waiting times are positively skewed.

blocks.prompt: Use the waiting-time histogram. How many patients waited less than $20$ minutes?
blocks.hint: Which bars lie to the left of $20$?
blocks.explain: The bars for $0 \le w < 10$ and $10 \le w < 20$ have heights $5$ and $12$, so $5 + 12 = 17$ patients.

blocks.prompt: A histogram of $34$ quiz scores, out of $50$, has five bars of equal width. From left to right, their heights are $2$, $4$, $7$, $12$ and $9$. Which describes the shape?
blocks.hint: On which side do the bars trail off slowly?

options.text: Positively skewed: the tail is to the right
Negatively skewed: the tail is to the left

blocks.explain: The peak is near the right, and the bars fall away slowly to the left. A tail on the left is negative skew: most students scored well.

blocks.text: A takeaway records the delivery times of $200$ orders. How many arrived within $20$ minutes? Add the frequencies of every class up to $20$.

blocks.statement: The [[cumulative-frequency|cumulative frequency]] at a value is the number of data values less than or equal to it: the running total of the frequencies.
blocks.plain: How many so far, counting up from the smallest value.

blocks.text: 1. Add a cumulative frequency column to the table.
2. Plot each cumulative frequency above the upper boundary of its class. Only there has every value in the class been counted.
3. Plot a first point at the lower boundary of the first class, with cumulative frequency $0$.
4. Join the points with a smooth curve or with straight lines. This lesson uses straight lines. A curve gives slightly different readings.

blocks.question: The delivery times of $200$ orders are shown in the table. $\begin{array}{c|c} \text{time, } t \text{ minutes} & \text{frequency} \\ \hline 10 < t \le 15 & 20 \\ 15 < t \le 20 & 40 \\ 20 < t \le 25 & 80 \\ 25 < t \le 30 & 40 \\ 30 < t \le 35 & 20 \end{array}$ Find the cumulative frequencies, and give the points to plot.
steps: Keep a running total, adding the next class each time.

$\begin{array}{c|c} t & \text{cumulative frequency} \\ \hline t \le 10 & 0 \\ t \le 15 & 20 \\ t \le 20 & 20 + 40 = 60 \\ t \le 25 & 60 + 80 = 140 \\ t \le 30 & 140 + 40 = 180 \\ t \le 35 & 180 + 20 = 200 \end{array}$
The last total is $200$, the number of orders. That is your check.

blocks.alt: Cumulative frequency graph of 200 delivery times. Straight lines join the points (10, 0), (15, 20), (20, 60), (25, 140), (30, 180) and (35, 200). Dashed lines go across from cumulative frequencies 50, 100 and 150 to the graph and then down to the time axis at 18.75, 22.5 and 26.25 minutes, labelled Q1, median and Q3.
blocks.caption: Read across from the cumulative frequency, then down to the time axis.

blocks.text: Now read the graph the other way. Half the data lies below the median. A quarter lies below the lower quartile $Q_{1}$, and three quarters below the upper quartile $Q_{3}$. So, with $n$ values, read across from these heights:

blocks.statement: The $k$th [[percentile|percentile]] is the value with $k\%$ of the data below it. On a cumulative frequency graph, read across from $\frac{k}{100} \times n$.
blocks.plain: So $Q_{1}$, the median and $Q_{3}$ are the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles.

blocks.text: The [[interquartile-range|interquartile range]] is the spread of the middle half of the data. It is in the formula booklet.
The range is the largest value minus the smallest. Grouped data hides the exact values, so estimate it from where the graph starts and ends: here $35 - 10 = 25$ minutes.

blocks.question: Use the cumulative frequency graph of the $200$ delivery times. (a) Estimate the median and the interquartile range. (b) The slowest $10\%$ of orders get a refund. Estimate $T$, the shortest delivery time that gets one. (c) Estimate $N$, the number of orders that took more than $28$ minutes.
steps: (a) The median is at $\frac{200}{2} = 100$. Read across and down: $22.5$ minutes. As a check, $100$ is halfway from $60$ to $140$, so the time is halfway from $20$ to $25$.
(b) The slowest $10\%$ lie above the $90$th percentile, at $\frac{90}{100} \times 200 = 180$. Read across and down: $T = 30$ minutes.
(c) Read up from $28$ and across: $164$ orders took $28$ minutes or less.
The graph counts orders at or below a time, so subtract from the total: $N = 200 - 164 = 36$.

blocks.text: Reading across from the wrong height. The graph counts values below, so for the top $10\%$ read across from $90\%$ of $n$. For “more than”, subtract your reading from $n$.

blocks.prompt: Use the delivery-times graph to find the $30$th percentile.
blocks.hint: Find $30\%$ of $200$ first, then read across.
blocks.explain: $\frac{30}{100} \times 200 = 60$. The graph reaches $60$ at $t = 20$, so the $30$th percentile is $20$ minutes.

blocks.prompt: Use the delivery-times graph. How many orders took more than $25$ minutes?
blocks.hint: The graph gives the number that took $25$ minutes or less.
blocks.explain: The graph gives $140$ orders at $25$ minutes or less, so $200 - 140 = 60$ took longer.

blocks.text: A box and whisker diagram, or box plot, draws five numbers to scale. It shows where the data starts and ends, and where its middle half sits.

blocks.statement: The [[five-number-summary|five-number summary]] is the smallest value, $Q_{1}$, the median, $Q_{3}$ and the largest value. A [[box-and-whisker-diagram|box and whisker diagram]] has a box from $Q_{1}$ to $Q_{3}$, a line at the median, and a whisker out from each side.
blocks.plain: The box holds the middle half of the data. The whiskers reach out to the rest.

blocks.text: 1. Draw a scale, then the box from $Q_{1}$ to $Q_{3}$ with a line at the median.
2. Find the fences $Q_{1} - 1.5 \times \mathrm{IQR}$ and $Q_{3} + 1.5 \times \mathrm{IQR}$ from {{lesson:4.1}}. Any value beyond them is an [[outlier|outlier]].
3. Draw each whisker to the most extreme value that is not an outlier, and mark each outlier with a cross.

blocks.alt: Box and whisker diagram on a length scale from 10 to 50 centimetres. The left whisker starts at 14. The box spans 22 to 30, and a line inside it marks the median, 26. The right whisker ends at 42, labelled largest non-outlier, and a cross at 47 is labelled outlier.
blocks.caption: Lengths of fish, in cm. The whisker stops at $42$, the longest fish that is not an outlier.

blocks.text: In the fish diagram, $Q_{1} = 22$ and $Q_{3} = 30$, so $\mathrm{IQR} = 8$ and $1.5 \times \mathrm{IQR} = 12$. The fences are $22 - 12 = 10$ and $30 + 12 = 42$.

No fish is shorter than $10$ cm, so the left whisker reaches the shortest fish, $14$ cm. A $42$ cm fish is not beyond the upper fence, so the right whisker ends there. The $47$ cm fish is beyond it, so it is a cross.

blocks.question: The number of items in each of $45$ online orders is shown in the table. $\begin{array}{c|ccccccccc} \text{items} & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 & 8 & 12 \\ \hline \text{frequency} & 4 & 9 & 11 & 8 & 6 & 3 & 2 & 1 & 1 \end{array}$ (a) Use your calculator to find $Q_1$, the median and $Q_3$. (b) Determine whether any value is an outlier. (c) Draw the box and whisker diagram.
steps: (a) Enter the items in one list and the frequencies in a second. Run one-variable statistics with the second list as the frequency list.
Write down what you read: smallest $1$, $Q_{1} = 2$, median $= 3$, $Q_{3} = 5$, largest $12$.
(b) $\mathrm{IQR} = 5 - 2 = 3$. The fences are $2 - 1.5 \times 3 = -2.5$ and $5 + 1.5 \times 3 = 9.5$.
Nothing is below $-2.5$. Only $12 > 9.5$, so the order of $12$ items is an outlier.
(c) The box runs from $2$ to $5$ with a line at $3$. The left whisker reaches $1$. The right whisker reaches $8$, the largest value that is not an outlier, and a cross marks $12$.

blocks.alt: Box and whisker diagram on a scale from 0 to 13 items. The left whisker runs from 1 to 2. The box spans 2 to 5, and a line inside it marks the median, 3. The right whisker runs from 5 to 8, and a cross marks 12.
blocks.caption: Items per order. The cross at $12$ is an outlier.

blocks.text: Leaving out the frequency list on the GDC. The calculator then treats the items as nine single values and gives the wrong quartiles.

Box plots are best for comparing two data sets on one scale. Make two comparisons, each in context: the medians for centre, and the IQRs or ranges for spread. A box plot doesn't show the mean, so don't compare means.

Shape matters too. If the median sits in the middle of the box and the whiskers are about the same length, the data is symmetric, so it may be normally distributed ({{lesson:4.9}}). A lopsided box or one long whisker means skewed data, which is unlikely to be normal.

blocks.alt: Two box and whisker diagrams on one test-mark scale from 30 to 90. Class A: whiskers from 30 to 84, box from 48 to 66, median 57; the box and whiskers are symmetric. Class B: whiskers from 35 to 78, box from 58 to 69, median 65; the left whisker is much longer than the right.
blocks.caption: Class A is symmetric. Class B has a long tail of low marks.

blocks.question: Two classes sat the same test. Class A's five-number summary is $30, 48, 57, 66, 84$, and class B's is $35, 58, 65, 69, 78$. (a) Find the IQR of each class. (b) Compare the two distributions. (c) State which class's marks may be normally distributed, with a reason.
steps: (b) Centre: class B's median, $65$, is higher than class A's, $57$. So class B generally scored higher.
Spread: class B's IQR, $11$, is smaller than class A's, $18$. So class B's marks were more consistent.
(c) Class A: the median is $9$ from each quartile and both whiskers are $18$ long. It is symmetric, so its marks may be normal. Class B's whiskers are $23$ and $9$ long, so its marks are skewed.

blocks.prompt: Scores in a quiz have $Q_{1} = 40$ and $Q_{3} = 52$. The three highest scores are $66$, $70$ and $71$. Where does the upper whisker end?
blocks.hint: Find the upper fence. Is a value equal to the fence an outlier?
blocks.explain: $\mathrm{IQR} = 12$, so the upper fence is $52 + 18 = 70$. $70$ is not an outlier, but $71$ is. The whisker ends at $70$, with a cross at $71$.

blocks.prompt: Each option is a five-number summary: smallest, $Q_{1}$, median, $Q_{3}$, largest. Which data set may be normally distributed?
blocks.hint: Compare the median's distance to each quartile, and the two whisker lengths.
blocks.explain: For $2, 5, 6, 7, 10$ the median is $1$ from each quartile and both whiskers are $3$ long, so it is symmetric. The first set has a long right whisker, and the last a long left whisker.

blocks.text: Class intervals are inequalities with no gaps, such as $20 \le t < 25$ and $25 \le t < 30$. A boundary value goes in the class whose inequality it satisfies.
In a histogram with equal class widths, bar height is frequency and the bars touch.
Plot cumulative frequency at each upper class boundary, starting from $0$ at the first lower boundary. It counts values at or below, so for “more than” subtract from $n$.

blocks.tex: \text{median at } \tfrac{n}{2}, \qquad Q_{1} \text{ at } \tfrac{n}{4}, \qquad Q_{3} \text{ at } \tfrac{3n}{4}, \qquad k\text{th percentile at } \tfrac{k}{100} \times n

blocks.text: Box plot: box from $Q_{1}$ to $Q_{3}$, line at the median, whiskers to the most extreme values that are not outliers, a cross for each outlier.
Compare medians for centre and IQRs for spread, in context. A symmetric box and whiskers means the data may be normal.

mistakes: Plotting cumulative frequency at class midpoints. Plot it at each upper class boundary.
Reading “more than” straight off a cumulative frequency graph. The graph counts values at or below, so subtract the reading from $n$. For the top $10\%$, read across from $90\%$ of $n$.
Drawing a whisker out to an outlier, or calling a value equal to a fence an outlier. Whiskers stop at the most extreme value that is not an outlier.
Leaving out the frequency list when entering a frequency table on the GDC. Each value then counts once, and the quartiles are wrong.
Comparing means from box plots. A box plot shows medians and quartiles, so compare those, in context.
examTips: Use the graph to estimate: write down the height you read across from, such as $\frac{n}{2}$ for the median, and draw the reading lines. That earns the method mark.
Draw a histogram or box plot: label the axes, use an even scale and plot accurately. Mark outliers with crosses.
Compare two distributions: one sentence on the medians and one on the IQRs, each with numbers and in context.
